conference.title: FloSports and Pac-12 Enter All-Encompassing Media Partnership to Bring the League’s Exclusive NCAA Wrestling Events to FloWrestling
conference.summary: FloSports and the Pac-12 Conference have entered into a historic media partnership that will bring all Pac-12 wrestling events to FloWrestling beginning with the 2026-27 season, providing a framework for future media agreements in the college space. The agreement makes FloWrestling the exclusive home to all Pac-12 wrestling for the next several seasons. The first Pac-12 events on FloWrestling will take place on Sunday,  Nov. 1, with more schedule information available at Pac-12.com.   The partnership will see all nine Pac-12 wrestling programs featured on FloWrestling for home meets, including Air Force, Cal Poly, Cal State Bakersfield, Little Rock, Northern Colorado, Northern Illinois, North Dakota State, Oregon State, and South Dakota State. Collectively these programs are rich with wrestling success boasting multiple NCAA Champions and dozens of All Americans in their history. This year the Pac-12 added five new teams to the conference making it an even more powerful player on the national stage.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga unanimously selected to win Pac-12 Conference in preseason media poll
Gonzaga.summary:
New league, same lofty expectations for a Gonzaga program that captured 27 regular-season championships and 23 conference tournament crowns during a 37-year residence in the West Coast Conference.

The Zags are expected to pick up right where they left off, selected as the unanimous favorite to win a Pac-12 Conference championship next spring by a panel of media members covering the league.

Gonzaga claimed each of the 17 first-place votes in the preseason poll released Thursday morning, just five days before Mark Few’s team opens the 2026-27 campaign with a juicy nonconference matchup against Matt Painter and Purdue.

Coming off its fourth straight NCAA Tournament appearance, Utah State was not surprisingly picked to finish second in the new conference, followed by No. 3 San Diego State, No. 4 Colorado State, No. 5 Oregon State, No. 6 Boise State, No. 7 Texas State, No. 8 Washington State and No. 9 Fresno State.

It continues a long run of preseason No. 1 nods for Gonzaga, which was picked to win the WCC every season since 2001, with the exception of the 2023-24 and 2017-18 seasons.

The 15th-ranked Zags were the only Pac-12 team to appear in the preseason Associated Press Top 25, but Utah State appeared on one AP ballot at No. 24, enough to earn two points in the poll.

Unlike other conferences, the Pac-12 did not release preseason all-conference teams, or announced a preseason player of the year, instead naming two players from each of the nine teams to the “2026-27 Men’s Basketball Impact List,” as selected by the league’s coaches.

Senior forward Braden Huff and sophomore wing Davis Fogle were Gonzaga’s selections – not unexpectedly, with both named to 20-player preseason watch lists for national positional awards this week. Fogle was named to the Julius Erving Small Forward watch list on Wednesday, one day before Huff was included on the watch list for the Karl Malone Power Forward award.

Huff had a 19-point, 11-rebound double-double in Gonzaga’s exhibition loss at Arkansas on Saturday and scored 11 points in 16 minutes during the team’s 91-59 victory over Lewis-Clark State. Fogle is just weeks removed from scoring 30 points in 20 minutes at Kraziness in the Kennel and had eight points against LCSC after missing the Arkansas exhibition with a left leg injury.

Washington State placed UNLV transfer Ladji Dembele and East Texas A&M transfer Ronnie Harrison on the Impact List. Harrison reached double figures in each of WSU’s two preseason exhibition games, scoring 23 points on 8 of 9 shooting in the Cougars’ 84-80 victory over cross-state rival Washington on Sunday.

Others named to the Impact List were Boise State’s Dovydas Butka and Damari Wheeler-Thomas, Colorado State’s Kyle Jorgensen and Jase Butler, Fresno State’s Bradey Henige and Ross Candelino, Oregon State’s Josiah Lake II and Daniel Freitag, San Diego State’s Elzie Harrington and Tae Simmons, Texas State’s Paul Djobet and DJ Hall and Utah State’s Mason Falslev and Dallin Hall.

Gonzaga.title: Texas judge tentatively denies TRO for Chauncey Wiggins; Gonzaga wing remains ineligible before season opener
Gonzaga.summary:
A judge in McLennan County, Texas, has tentatively denied a temporary restraining order for Chauncey Wiggins and other player plaintiffs seeking a fifth year of eligibility, likely keeping the Gonzaga wing out of Monday’s season opener against Purdue in Las Vegas.

Wiggins and other athletes made a late push to join a lawsuit filed in Waco, Texas, against the NCAA after attempts to seek injunctive relief in other 5-in-5 lawsuits were unsuccessful.

The Gonzaga wing sought an alternate route to eligibility after a stay was granted in his Georgia lawsuit on Sept. 9. Wiggins and other players in the Georgia lawsuit, including Arizona forward RJ Godfrey and Boise State guard Lamar Washington, moved to withdraw their names from the case earlier this week and filed to join a group of athletes that previously received an injunction in the Wheeler v. NCAA case in Texas.

Presiding over the case, Judge Ryan Luna of the 414th Judicial District Court listened to arguments from both sides Thursday morning before tentatively denying the TRO for Wiggins and other plaintiffs applying for late inclusion.

At the end of a two-hour ruling, Luna granted an appearance for the group of players seeking inclusion in Wheeler v. NCAA, but denied a TRO for Wiggins and plaintiffs currently under stays in other state jurisdictions. Luna said he’d sign an order rejecting the TRO, “unless something in the briefing overwhelms me.” He gave the plaintiffs’ attorneys until 10 p.m. to file a briefing.

“Those players that you can identify that have already gone through this process on these merits, who have sought injunctive relief from another state court or granted it, I think we talked about Tennessee and Georgia,” Luna said. “Any of those players we can identify, I’m going to deny the TRO on those.”

It’s unclear what additional legal options exist for Wiggins, who could be on Gonzaga’s bench Monday afternoon while fellow 5-in-5 transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida) and Javon Bennett (Dayton) – currently eligible through legal decisions in California and Ohio – suit up against the Boilermakers in the season opener.

Godfrey committed to Arizona and former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd late in the offseason, but Thursday’s ruling means he also won’t be able to compete against UCLA in the second game of Monday’s doubleheader, which tips off at 7 p.m. in Vegas.

During Thursday’s hearing, Ryan Downton of Texas Trial Group, an attorney who’s representing a handful of athletes across the country in various 5-in-5 lawsuits, argued athletes would face irreparable harm if they weren’t able to obtain a fifth year of eligibility, citing the loss of scholarship, as well as name, image and likeness (NIL) and professional exposure.

“It does come down to the athletes and if the court believes the players are likely to prevail and suffer irreparable harm if they’re not permitted to play and there’s limited or no harm to the NCAA, if the court accepts the players should be here, the court should grant the injunction,” Downton said. “And the court should not penalize the players for availing themselves of their procedural rights any more than the NCAA should be punished to appeal decisions it doesn’t like.

“It ultimately comes down to the athletes. For any players before the court, is it equitable they play while this plays out, or is it equitable that they don’t?”

An NCAA attorney raised the issue of breach of contract, arguing any state’s law should govern the interpretation of that contract, and contending athletes from other lawsuits shouldn’t have the option to jump from one 5-in-5 case to the next.

“These plaintiffs are judicially estopped when coming in and saying that Texas substantive contract law should be applied to their contract claim, because they’ve already gone to Tennessee and Georgia to say substantive Tennessee and Georgia law applies to my breach of contract claim,” the NCAA attorney said. “So we can’t bring in Texas law here. … You’ve got to act in good faith, which would necessarily require you honor and respect the orders of other courts as opposed to just go somewhere else and say, ‘Well I didn’t really mean that Georgia and Tennessee law applies to my contract. I actually meant Texas was because that didn’t go the way I wanted it to.’ ”

Wiggins played three seasons at Clemson and one more at Florida State, averaging 13.3 points and 3.9 rebounds while making 38.7% from the 3-point line last year with the Seminoles. Before the fifth-year option was presented as a possibility, Wiggins joined the Boston Celtics at NBA Summer League, logging 8.3 minutes over three appearances in Las Vegas.

The 6-foot-11 wing made a pair of 3s and scored eight points during Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel scrimmage, but wasn’t eligible to suit up for the team’s exhibition games, on Saturday at Arkansas and Wednesday against NAIA Lewis-Clark State at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Bennett still eligible

Hours after Wiggins’ TRO was denied, Gonzaga got a positive update on the 5-in-5 eligibility front.

Bennett, one of three point guards that could see time in Few’s rotation this season, remains on track to play in Monday’s opener after the Ohio Supreme Court considered supplemental briefs from both parties in the Borovicanin v. NCAA lawsuit, keeping a previous ruling in effect.

Players in the case obtained a preliminary injunction in July, clearing them for a fifth season of eligibility, but a lower court issued a stay that temporarily overturned the original decision. A higher court then stayed that ruling earlier this month, reinstating the plaintiffs’ eligibility.

The Ohio Supreme Court examined the legality and the effect of an executive order issued on Oct. 13 by Ohio Governor Mike DeWine extending a fifth year of eligibility to athletes planning to compete at Ohio institutions in 2026-27. DeWine was sued by the NCAA in federal court, with the governing body arguing the decision would make it “impossible for all schools to compete on a level playing field.”

According to Thursday’s case announcement, “The order of the Hamilton County Common Please Court remains in effect pending this court’s consideration of the memorandum in support of jurisdiction.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Massamba Diop closes strong, Parker Jefferson impresses during LCSC exhibition | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
If Gonzaga fans didn’t overreact to a 76-72 loss at Arkansas on Saturday, it’s probably safe to apply the same approach to Wednesday’s 91-59 victory over NAIA Lewis-Clark State.

The 15th-ranked Zags got just about everything they wanted and needed from their final dress rehearsal and now look forward to Monday’s high-profile season opener against Purdue in Las Vegas.

What the Zags have in front of them is decidedly more exciting than what’s in the rearview mirror, but we’ll still take an opportunity to review three topics and storylines from Wednesday’s exhibition before moving on to Monday’s nationally-televised opener at T-Mobile Arena.

Still processing

It’s been trial by fire for Massamba Diop through Gonzaga’s exhibition slate.

Gonzaga’s prized transfer portal pickup encountered foul trouble in both preseason games, was caught trying to trip Razorbacks forward Miika Muurinen in a sequence that resulted in technical fouls for both players and, above all else, is still adjusting to a new role in Mark Few’s system, with mixed results against Arkansas and LCSC.

The 7-foot-1 Diop conceded the opening tip to 6-foot-9 LCSC forward Dallon Morgan on Wednesday, but subsequently provided one of the game’s top highlights when he turned away Brandon Suber’s layup attempts three minutes into the opening frame, drawing a loud reaction from the home crowd.

Diop pulled down two defensive rebounds but committed his second and third fouls over a 15-second stretch that, in many ways, characterized his first two outings in a Gonzaga uniform.

After sitting the final eight minutes of the first half, Diop started in the second and made immediate contributions. The towering center scooped up an offensive rebound while picking himself up off the ground, maneuvered around L-C’s Dylan Skaife and jammed the ball into the basket.

“I think Massamba’s doing a decent job of protecting the basket for the most part right now, which is kind of what we haven’t had in awhile,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said. “I think he needs to continue to keep working on rebounding and catching and finishing him. The guards are finding him now. He’s playing with some good guards that can really manipulate ball screens and situations. He’s just got to slow down and catch the ball and finish. I think that’s kind of the next area of growth.”

Diop’s second-half turnaround was encouraging. The Arizona State transfer had eight of his 10 points after the break, finishing 5 of 7 from the field with five rebounds, one blocked shot and one steal.

“I think every day you see growth with him,” Braden Huff said. “It’s undeniable, his athleticism and length and his skill. Once we just get him to learn the system and what we need out of him the sky is the limit for him. He’s going to be really good for us.”

Jefferson shines

Gonzaga picked up scoring and rebounding contributions from many of the usual suspects on Wednesday, but there were also a few surprises on the final stat sheet.

Parker Jefferson, for example, matched teammate Izan Almansa and LCSC’s Titus Yearout for a game-high 12 points on 6 of 9 shooting. Jefferson also led all players with six rebounds and two blocked shots to go with his two assists and one steal.

Jefferson enters the regular season as the fourth or fifth member of Gonzaga’s frontcourt rotation behind Huff, Diop, Almansa and potentially freshman center Sam Funches, but the sophomore forward has delivered in both of his exhibition stints, making 3 of 4 free throws at Arkansas with two rebounds and one steal in just under four minutes of action. Jefferson, whose mother Carrie played basketball at Arkansas and father Mike played for the Razorbacks’ offensive line, had a cheering section of nearly 40 family members and friends at Bud Walton Arena.

In Wednesday’s postgame presser, Gonzaga’s coach praised Jefferson for his connectivity, and not necessarily just on the court.

“Parker’s done a nice job. I’ll tell you what he’s done a really nice job of is helping us bring the team together,” Few said. “We didn’t have many returnees and he’s done a great job of welcoming everybody in and making them comfortable and just kind of being a great teammate, so obviously it’s nice to be able to reward him with some moments like that.”

More than ball

More than two months after destructive wildfires displaced thousands of Spokane residents, Gonzaga and LCSC agreed their preseason exhibition could be a good opportunity to raise funds for those rebuilding homes and replacing items lost from the blazes.

A portion of the money from ticket sales on Wednesday went toward Phase 2 of the Karen Worthy Memorial Grant, a nonprofit created to help those impacted by the Spokane Complex fires rebuild.

“I think this has been a really great opportunity for me to talk to the guys about, hey these are people that are watching us on TV every game, these are people that are coming to our games, these are people that are wanting to meet you in the restaurants or see you walking around town,” Few said. “I think it was really important that we kind of stepped up and again, kind of raised the awareness. Sometimes when you have events like this, everybody wants to run out and feels horrible about it and wants to give, but then as time goes on it starts waning and dissipating. I want us to kind of make another statement that hey, there’s still need out there right now.”

LCSC also chipped in to assist with the cause, donating its $5,000 game check to the Karen Worthy Grant. Warriors coach Austin Johnson had extended family members evacuated and one friend who lost his home as a result of fire damage.

“There’s tons of fees that aren’t really realized when you’re having to rebuild your whole house and home, or just anything that’s taken away with something like this,” Few said. “We’re happy to help and we’re hopeful because our guys are stepping up, myself and our guys are going to make a sizeable dent in this. Hopefully other people will step up and follow along with us. Everybody, there’s still a huge, huge need and the insurances and all this doesn’t cover everything so that’s what we’re trying to do.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women picked to win new Pac-12; WSU selected sixth | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
With five starters and five other returners, it is no surprise that the Gonzaga women’s basketball team was tapped to win the Pac-12 Conference championship in a media poll released Thursday.

The Bulldogs’ top seven scorers return from a team that finished 24-10 and won the West Coast Conference title in its final season in the league.

Oregon State was picked to finish second in the remodeled conference. The Beavers may have been picked second based on their reputation and penchant for postseason success. In the final year of the original Pac-12 (2023-24), they advanced to the Elite Eight.

San Diego State, which won the Mountain West championship last year, was picked third followed by Colorado State, Boise State, Washington State, Fresno State, Texas State and Utah State.

Gonzaga received 16 of 19 first-place votes. Oregon State received one and San Diego State received two.

Colorado State won the MW Tournament last year and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

WSU returns six players who started at various times. The Cougars have much to prove after stumbling to a 9-25 record last year.

ESPN released its preseason bracketology compiled by Charlie Creme Monday. Gonzaga is picked as the automatic qualifier from the Pac-12 as a 10 seed. Oregon State and San Diego State are picked in the new 76-team field to play play-in games.

Players to watch

The Pac-12 also released its Preseason Impact List.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker, the WCC Player and Freshman of the Year last season, and junior guard Allie Turner, a WCC First Team selection a year ago, were two of 18 players named. Each school was allowed to nominate two players.

Named from WSU are seniors Alex Covill (post) and Eleonora Villa (guard), a WCC Second Team pick last year.

Former WSU guard Jenna Villa and point guard Kennedie Shuler were selected from Oregon State. Shuler was the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and Villa was a First Team selection.

Add to the list

Gonzaga’s Whittaker was named to two more watch lists.

Whittaker, from Christchurch, New Zealand, is on the Naismith Trophy Women’s College Player of the Year preseason list along with the Katrina McClain Award preseason list. On Tuesday she was named to the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason list.

She is one of two Pac-12 players on the Hammon list.

In her first season playing for the Zags a year ago, Whittaker averaged 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game with 649 points and a school-record 348 rebounds.

Coach list

Lisa Fortier, who is entering her 13th season as head coach at Gonzaga, has been named to the Kathy Delaney-Smith Coach of the Year preseason watch list.

Fortier is one of 20 coaches nationally selected to the preseason list. The award is in its fourth season.

She enters the season four wins away from becoming the all-time winningest Gonzaga coach with a 313-84 overall record. That’s a .788 winning percentage. The winningest coach is Kelly Graves (316-136, .699), who is beginning his 13th season at Oregon.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga distributes 'meaningful minutes' to variety of players during 91-59 exhibition victory
Gonzaga.summary:
Mark Few would usually zero in on things like field goal percentage, rebounding or turnovers. With NAIA Lewis-Clark State visiting for Wednesday’s exhibition, Gonzaga’s coach was focused on another statistical column when judging whether the team’s final preseason tune-up was ultimately a success.

No, not final score. Gonzaga was expected to win in runaway fashion and had no issue, cruising past LCSC 91-59 at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Few’s eyes shifted to another section of the final stat sheet: minutes played. Everybody on Gonzaga’s roster registered at least four, with only one player, point guard Javon Bennett, exceeding 20 during Wednesday’s exhibition rout.

Another positive? The Zags left the Kennel without any injury concerns and should have everyone who played Wednesday available for Monday’s 4:30 p.m. (TNT/HBO Max) showdown with Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

“I think the best thing is we were able to get everybody in and get them kind of substantial minutes,” said Few, who wasn’t able to disperse playing time as liberally during a tightly contested exhibition loss at Arkansas on Saturday. “The other night, kind of the way it was going, you probably didn’t get as many guys in as you’d like, meaningful minutes. So getting everybody meaningful minutes tonight was probably the best thing.”

Scoring balance might have been a close second.

Gonzaga’s leading scorers, Parker Jefferson and Izan Almansa, both finished with 12 points but nine players had at least six. Joining Jefferson and Almansa in the double-digit club were Braden Huff and Bennett, who had 11 points apiece, along with Massamba Diop, who overcame a slow start to add 10.

Even in a dominant preseason win, though, Few was able to poke holes and identify shortcomings. The Zags were improved but still below-average from the perimeter, making 9 of 27 (33%) four days after a dismal 6 of 28 (214%) showing at Arkansas.

They won the rebounding column, but Few felt the 41-36 disparity should’ve been more substantial given the height, size and athleticism advantage Gonzaga still had over its NAIA opponent at nearly every position on the floor – even when Few’s reserves were in the game.

“Rebounding is something, we haven’t been good in the preseason here,” Few said. “Didn’t exactly do a great job tonight. We battled at Arkansas against a really good, big team but it’s something we’ve always got to take to heart because it’s going to be a big key to our season.”

Davis Fogle returned to Gonzaga’s starting lineup after taking precautionary measures and sitting out with a left leg injury against Arkansas. The sophomore wing played just 16 minutes, but was effective at both ends of the floor, scoring eight points on 4-of-9 shooting to go with two rebounds, two assists and two steals.

Gonzaga made its first two 3-pointers out of the gates, from starting guards Xaivian Lee and Isiah Harwell, and put together an impressive three-possession stretch minutes later when Diop blocked an LCSC shot into the first row, Harwell collected an offensive rebound before going back up for a dunk and Fogle converted on a steal-and-score sequence to extend a 7-0 run.

The Zags lost control of the game for a brief stretch after that, making a hockey substitution that saw the five starters replaced by five newcomers: Bennett, Nathan De Sousa, Luca Foster, Almansa and Sam Funches.

Fueled by seven straight points from Idaho transfer Titus Yearout, the Warriors went on an 8-0 run to close the deficit to 23-18 with 11 minutes, 11 seconds to play. But Gonzaga outscored its opponent 31-9 to close the frame and went into halftime with a 54-27 advantage.

Yearout led the Lewiston-based Warriors with 12 points, making 4 of 14 shots from the field and 2 of 6 from the 3-point line. Dylan Skaife, a Ferris High School product, scored five points on 2 of 7 from the field and 1 of 6 from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga’s bench, led by Izan Almansa, contributes in exhibition blowout
Gonzaga.summary:
Izan Almansa received his eligibility just six days ago, but his intuitive play on the court makes it seem like he’s been in a Gonzaga uniform for a few years.

The 6-foot-10, 220-pound forward from Spain has been solid off the bench in a pair of exhibition games, including a 12-point effort in the first half of the Zags’ 91-59 exhibition rout over NAIA Lewis-Clark State College on Wednesday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

The NCAA cleared Almansa on Friday, just before the team departed for Arkansas. One day later, Almansa was one of the most productive Zags, scoring 14 points in a 76-72 loss to 15th-ranked Arkansas in Fayetteville.

“It was right before the flight, coach (Stephen) Gentry told me,” Almansa said. “I wasn’t expecting to play. Everyone on the team got so hyped, me too. It was a really good moment.”

Almansa, who played for the NBA G League Ignite in 2023-24 and spent last season with Real Madrid in Spain’s Liga ACB, is on track to be the first big off the bench behind Braden Huff and Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop.

“He’s just got a very good feel for the game, so when you have that, everybody plays better with you and the game becomes a little easier for everybody,” head coach Mark Few said. “He knows when to pass, he understands spacing, he knows how to find his own shot.

“He’s just a really skilled basketball player. Those guys are always great to have on the floor from a coach’s perspective and also to play with.”

Almansa made 6 of 9 shots, including 1 of 2 3-pointers, against the talented Razorbacks. He hit 4 of 5 field-goal attempts, 2 of 2 on 3s, against LCSC.

“He’s obviously played against some really good players, some pros, in his time,” Huff said. “He’s super smart, athletic, quick. He’s a lot of fun to play with. I think he gives defenses a different look and he’s also really good on defense. He’ll be another big piece for us.”

Almansa was part of a GU bench that sputtered when five subs entered at the 14-minute mark of the first half. The Zags’ 11-point lead melted to seven before the starting unit returned.

The bench’s second run was a different story, outscoring the Warriors 18-2, boosting GU’s halftime lead to 54-27.

“Everyone was welcoming me great, knowing I wasn’t eligible at first,” said Almansa, whose first name is pronounced E-thun. “So it was a little bit hard, but everybody helped me, gave me a lot of confidence from my coaches, teammates, everybody here.”

Sophomore forward Parker Jefferson had nice stretches in each half and finished with 12 points, six rebounds, two assists and two blocks.

“I’m really proud of Parker,” said Huff, who scored 11 points in just 16 minutes. “He gave us good minutes (against Arkansas) and tonight he also did good things out there. I told him, I’ve been there coming off a redshirt year where you’re finally playing. I just told him to be ready regardless of what his role is night in and night out.”

Dayton transfer Javon Bennett, who had a tough shooting night (1 of 8) vs. Arkansas, chipped in 11 points, including three 3-pointers, and two assists against the visitors from Lewiston. Freshman guard Juwan Ekanga, a 6-6 freshman guard, added seven points, four rebounds and three assists. Gonzaga’s bench produced 47 points.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Chauncey Wiggins withdraws from Georgia 5-in-5 lawsuit, will pursue injunction in Texas
Gonzaga.summary:
Seeking expedited relief in his ongoing eligibility battle, Gonzaga transfer Chauncey Wiggins has withdrawn his name from a 5-in-5 lawsuit in the state of Georgia and will now pursue a legal injunction in Texas with the Bulldogs’ season opener just five days away.

Wiggins initially secured a fifth year of eligibility through a preliminary injunction in Georgia, but the NCAA subsequently filed for a stay that reversed the decision, making the former Florida State and Clemson player ineligible.

The Superior Court of Cobb County in Georgia recently set arguments for Jan. 12, 2027, which would’ve sidelined Wiggins through Gonzaga’s nonconference schedule as well as multiple Pac-12 Conference games, with no guarantee he’d receive an injunction.

Wiggins was one of 16 players who chose to withdraw from the case, according to a notice of voluntary dismissal without prejudice filed Tuesday by Cobb County Superior Court Clerk Henry Thompson. The group also includes RJ Godfrey, one of Wiggins’ former teammates at Clemson and someone expected to be a major contributor for former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd at Arizona, should he secure a fifth-year waiver.

Wiggins will continue to seek legal relief in another jurisdiction, applying to join a group of player plaintiffs in the Wheeler v. NCAA case taking place in McLennan County, Texas. Other player plaintiffs in the case – Baylor football player Hosea Wheeler, Texas Tech forward Darrion Williams, Utah State guard Dallin Hall and former Washington State guard Nate Calmese to name a few – were granted a preliminary injunction in September, clearing them to play until at least Dec. 14 when the case goes to trial.

An intervention hearing will take place at 7:30 a.m. on Thursday in Waco, Texas, to determine whether Wiggins and other members of the Godfrey v. NCAA will be added in the case and whether they’ll be eligible for the injunction that was extended to player plaintiffs in the original lawsuit.

The wing’s outside shooting would be a valuable weapon for Gonzaga if he’s cleared to play. Wiggins made a career-high 72 3s last season at Florida State, shooting at a 38.7% clip. He contributed to the 3-point shooting barrage at Kraziness in the Kennel, making 2 of his 5 attempts, but wasn’t eligible to suit up for Saturday’s exhibition at Arkansas, watching from the bench in a team sweatsuit as the Zags struggled from distance, finishing just 6 of 28.

Wiggins didn’t play in GU’s second exhibition on Wednesday against Lewis-Clark State, but fed passes to teammates during pregame warmups and was an active member of the bench during a comfortable win at McCarthey Athletic Center.

“He’s practicing every day and he’s been great,” Few said. “He’s been great, working out, looks good. Obviously would really help him when we hopefully do get him eligible here.”

In his lone season at Florida State, Wiggins averaged 13.3 points per game and 3.9 rebounds, shooting 47.9% from the field. He spent the three prior seasons at Clemson, starting in 43 of the 70 games as a sophomore and junior. Wiggins averaged 8.3 ppg during his junior season and 5.4 ppg as a sophomore.

Wiggins is one of three Zags who’ve taken legal action against the NCAA to secure a fifth year of eligibility. Xaivian Lee and Javon Bennett are eligible for the moment, but both still could face potential obstacles in lawsuits taking place in California and Ohio.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, LCSC made late push to schedule charity exhibition that will benefit Spokane wildfire victims
Gonzaga.summary:
With Gonzaga still in need of a second exhibition game last month, fourth-year assistant coach RJay Barsh made a familiar phone call right down the road.

Lewis-Clark State had always been game to make the two-hour trip north from Lewiston, visiting on three occasions under ninth-year coach Austin Johnson. It provides a unique opportunity for LCSC’s players to experience a top-15 college basketball heavyweight inside the Kennel and doubles as a chance for select members of Johnson’s roster to see friends and family in the Spokane area. For Gonzaga, it’s a solid tuneup against a competitive NAIA program that’s won 72% of its games under Johnson, a two-time NABC NAIA Coach of the Year.

Just one problem this year. The Warriors were completely booked. The NAIA has stringent scheduling limits and the Warriors didn’t have the flexibility to sneak another exhibition game onto their calendar.

Barsh had a potential solution, suggesting Gonzaga and Lewis-Clark State pitch the matchup as a charity exhibition that would raise money for Spokane wildfire victims. Johnson got to work on a petition that was submitted and subsequently approved by the NAIA.

The game is scheduled to tip off 6 p.m. Wednesday at McCarthey Athletic Center and will air locally on KHQ.

A generous and selfless gesture from LCSC’s coach followed. Johnson told Gonzaga to keep the $5,000 check the Warriors would receive from the exhibition and donate it to the Karen Worthy Memorial Wildfire Grant, a fund Bulldogs coach Mark Few helped launch to help families impacted by the Spokane Complex fires.

The amount isn’t insignificant to an NAIA program like LCSC – “a lot of money for us,” Johnson assured – but the Warriors’ coach had a personal connection to the wildfires and was happy to reroute the money to a good cause.

Johnson’s in-laws evacuated their Indian Trail home and watched numerous structures in their neighborhood disappear in the flames. Former LCSC forward Jared Tikker, an executive director of John Stockton’s Warehouse facility and the cousin of Johnson’s wife, Kelli, was forced to leave his home in Five Mile. Johnson’s close friend Jeremy Groth, the men’s basketball coach at Spokane Colleges, wasn’t as fortunate and lost his home in the fires.

“That’s one of the ways we’re getting the game is we promised the NAIA, we’re losing money, we’re spending money on gas and meals to go up there,” Johnson said. “We’re not making money. For me, it wasn’t just about getting the GU game, it was this can also be a good, positive thing.”

The objective for LCSC once the ball is tipped is the same as it was when the teams last played in 2024. No injuries, put together a few competitive stretches and give 40 minutes of effort, regardless of how lopsided the score gets.

“Last time we played them, we lost by 38, which that’s not something we do at LC State,” Johnson said. “So obviously you walk off the court and you feel like you are the worst team ever. I went back and looked and they have 14 or 15 wins by 38 or more since we played them. In retrospect, you look back and say maybe it isn’t that bad.”

LCSC has drawn the short stick over the years, often being the first opponent to get a glimpse of Gonzaga’s All-American frontcourt pairings before they’re introduced to the rest of the country in high-profile, nationally televised nonconference games.

Graham Ike and Braden Huff combined to score 45 points the last time the teams met in 2024, fueling the Zags to a 96-58 victory. Three years earlier, LCSC got an early preview of the Drew Timme-Chet Holmgren pairing that would help Gonzaga secure a top overall seed five months later at the NCAA Tournament. In 2019, Filip Petrusev and Anton Watson hurt the Warriors for 50 points in a 116-62 rout for the Zags.

On Wednesday night, LCSC will have to go through 7-1 Massamba Diop to score in the paint and deal with Huff’s polished post game when the Zags are on offense. Izan Almansa’s rebounding presents another issue off Few’s bench.

“Obviously they’re really good, because they haven’t asked us this year about what we’re going to do on ball screen coverage or this or that,” Johnson said. “So I don’t think I’m too worried about our X’s and O’s this year.”

Johnson knows his team can’t match up from a size or athleticism standpoint, but he’ll be encouraged if the Warriors manufacture 8-12 total minutes of “really, really competitive basketball.” He has fond memories of the trip in 2019. Well, the opening minutes of it. LCSC and Gonzaga were tied at 11-11 before Few switched to a pressing defense, sparking a 28-2 Bulldogs run.

“For us, we want to play hard,” Johnson said. “Not that Mark Few probably lays awake at night thinking about the LC State Warriors or anything like that, but I’d like to think one of the reasons we get asked back is we’re going to try to run some decent stuff. We want this to be good for them, too. I’d like to think we’ve been competitive enough to give them a look, but also they can try different rotations.”

LCSC’s Dylan Skaife, a junior who played under former GU forward Sean Mallon at Ferris High, is coming off an all-conference season with the Warriors. The sharpshooting guard, Johnson’s top returning scorer at 12.5 points per game, was the only Warrior to start in all 32 games last season and led the Cascade Conference in 3-pointers made with 90. That number also ranks fourth in a single season at LCSC.

“Can really shoot it, is our returning leading scorer, is off to a good start this year,” Johnson said. “I expect big things from him.”

Gonzaga.title: For No. 11 Gonzaga, clearance from the courts looms large | Wilner's Preseason Top 25
Gonzaga.summary:
Projecting the fate of basketball teams across the Division I landscape, extraordinarily difficult in the transfer portal era, is more challenging by an order of magnitude this fall because of unresolved eligibility lawsuits.

Days before the 2026-27 season openers, the coaches don’t even know who’s playing and who’s sitting in the aftermath of the NCAA’s controversial five-for-five ruling in the spring.

“We have a court system in the U.S. and that’s going to impact our game this year,” Arizona coach Tommy Lloyd said last week at the Big 12’s preseason media event. “You just wish cooler heads would prevail, and give these kids the opportunity they deserve.”

Well, sure, but college basketball has never been a place for cool heads, logical decisions and thoughtful strategy.

As a result, we’re left to guess at the roster composition for myriad preseason favorites that are awaiting final decisions from the courts.

Alas, onward and upward.

Here’s my preseason Associated Press ballot (with comments added):

1. Florida: An easy call given the loaded list of returnees and coach Todd Golden’s deft touch. The frontcourt is sublime with Alex Condon, Thomas Haugh and Rueben Chinyelu, and the backcourt should be one of the best in the SEC. If they stay healthy, the 2025 national champs could make it two titles in three years.

2. Illinois: Despite the departure of star point guard Keaton Wagler, the Illini were not one-hit wonders with their run to the Final Four. Guard Andrej Stojakovic and forward David Mirkovic lead a veteran core that adds Providence transfer Stefan Vaaks.

3. Duke: Proven playmakers, elite recruits and one superstar transfer, John Blackwell (from Wisconsin), form what should be another title contender for coach Jon Scheyer. (Editor’s note: These rankings are specific to the regular season and not based on teams finding new and preposterous ways to blow leads in the NCAA Tournament.)

4. UConn: Yes, the Huskies were hit hard by attrition with the departures of Tarris Reed and Alex Karaban and with Solo Ball taking a medical redshirt. But the most important piece is back: coach Dan Hurley. Add guards Silas Demary and Braylon Mullins and we’re quite confident the sum will exceed the parts.

5. Tennessee: With an elite transfer class that includes VCU’s Terrence Hill, Wake Forest’s Juke Harris and Notre Dame’s Jalen Haralson — it might be the best in the land — the Volunteers are set for another commendable but fruitless attempt to become a basketball school.

6. Michigan State: The return of star guard Jeremy Fears cemented Michigan State’s status as a Big Ten favorite alongside Illinois. Whether the Spartans return to the Final Four for the first time since 2019 depends on the production level from everyone else.

7. Arizona: The Wildcats might have the best frontline west of Gainesville, Florida, with Ivan Kharchenkov, Motiejus Krivas and RJ Godfrey, the Clemson transfer whose eligibility remains uncertain. But for the Wildcats to replicate their 2025-26 success, the unproven backcourt must blossom – and Arizona won’t have Jaden Bradley to light the path.

8. Louisville: The Cardinals possess the No. 2-ranked transfer class in the country (behind St. John’s) with Oregon point guard Jackson Shelstad, Kansas big man Flory Bidunga, Arkansas wing Karter Knox and Iowa forward Alvaro Folgueiras. If Seth Trimble (North Carolina) remains eligible, coach Pat Kelsey will have everything needed for a deep run in March.

9. Arkansas: As usual, coach John Calipari landed a stellar freshman class with four five-star prospects, including the No. 1 wing in the country, Jordan Smith. But anyone who watched the Razorbacks last season knows defense was not a priority. Unless that changes, the Hogs won’t reach their lofty potential.

10. Texas: Could this be the year Sean Miller finally reaches the Final Four? His incoming class of recruits and transfers is one of the best in the land with guards Isaiah Johnson (Colorado) and Mikey Lewis (Saint Mary’s) and forward David Punch (TCU). If the Longhorns are healthy, there are no excuses.

11. Gonzaga: With Davis Fogle, Braden Huff and Massamba Diop, the Zags possess a frontline that compares favorably to those at Arizona and Florida. The backcourt? Who knows. Coach Mark Few has several gifted players awaiting clearance from the court system. If the legal outcomes are unfriendly, the journey through the rebuilt Pac-12 could prove arduous.

12. St. John’s: Another school with major unresolved eligibility issues, although Baylor transfer Tounde Yessoufou is set to play and could have a massive impact. And unlike the other 364 schools in Division I, the Red Storm have Rick Pitino.

13. USC: This placement is based, in part, on Eric Musselman being a Year 3 coach. He led Nevada to the Sweet 16 in his third season in Reno and Arkansas to the Elite Eight in his third season in Fayetteville. Everything is set for success with returnees Rodney Rice, Alijah Arenas and Jacob Cofie, plus blue-chip recruits and a solid collection of transfers.

14. Houston: This is the first time the Cougars have not appeared in the Hotline’s preseason top 10 since we-can’t-remember-when. Joseph Tugler’s return should spur the harrowing defense, but the offense must be rebuilt around point guard Dedan Thomas, who averaged 15 points for LSU, and returning wings Mercy Miller and Chase McCarty.

15. Vanderbilt: Point guard Tyler Tanner’s decision to withdraw from the NBA draft at the deadline was one of the most significant in the country, offering the Commodores a chance to remain relevant. The transfer class features high-scoring former Washington State guard Ace Glass.

16. Nebraska: Many of the low-profile players who led the Cornhuskers to their greatest season are returning, with leading scorer Pryce Sandfort atop that list. But how will everyone associated with the program manage the expectations that are present in Lincoln for the first time in forever?

17. Alabama: Coach Nate Oats has proven adept at assimilating disparate parts rapidly. Combine returnee Aden Holloway with uber-recruit Jaxson Richardson and transfer Drew Fielder (Boise State), and the Crimson Tide has a core that can flourish.

18. Miami: The momentum continues for second-year coach Jai Lucas, who led the Hurricanes to 26 wins in his rookie year and landed two top transfers in Georgia center Somto Cyril and Villanova guard Acaden Lewis.

19. Virginia: The Cavaliers possess the NIL game necessary to compete for elite talent and a top-tier position in the ACC. Leading scorer Thijs De Ridder is returning. Add UC Irvine transfer Jurian Dixon, and coach Ryan Odom has a conference title contender.

20. Michigan: Coach Dusty May’s departure to the NBA was one of several offseason gut punches the 2026 national champions were forced to absorb. (They also lost star recruit Brandon McCoy to a season-ending injury.) Defending a title is never easy. In Michigan’s case, it will be brutally difficult.

21. Kansas: The decision to accept Purdue transfer Trey Kaufman-Renn, who was drafted and played in the NBA summer league, was deplorable. (His eligibility isn’t guaranteed.) The basketball gods will render judgment, and it won’t be pleasant for the Jayhawks. Not for nothing: Although Kaufman-Renn’s return doesn’t technically violate Big 12 rules, it violates the spirit of the August decision to ban professionals.

22. Saint Louis: Most of the key pieces to coach Josh Schertz’s 29-win machine are back. (So, too, is Schertz.) St. John’s and Gonzaga should be the best of the non-football schools next season, with the Billikens No. 3.

23. North Carolina: Michael Malone is a first-rate coach whose adjustment to the college game could take two months. That leaves three for the Tar Heels to excel.

24. Iowa: There’s a case for Ben McCollum as the top NCAA Tournament coach in the sport not named Dan Hurley, but these rankings are based on the regular season. And without court maestro Bennett Stirtz, the Hawkeyes might encounter a few potholes.

25. VCU: The Atlantic 10 could be the best of the mid-major conferences with VCU and Saint Louis leading the charge to relevance.

Also considered: BYU, Indiana, Iowa State, Kentucky, Miami (Ohio), Missouri, New Mexico, Ohio State, Purdue, San Diego State, Santa Clara, Syracuse, TCU, Texas A&M, Texas Tech, UCLA, Utah State, Villanova and Wisconsin

Gonzaga.title: Five former Gonzaga players named to NBA G League rosters for 2026-27 season
Gonzaga.summary:
Twelve former Gonzaga players appeared on NBA opening day rosters and five more could be one call away as they open the 2026-27 season in the NBA’s G League.

Two members of last year’s Gonzaga team, Jalen Warley and Tyon Grant-Foster, will start their professional careers in the G League, along with another trio of former Bulldogs that includes Anton Watson, Nolan Hickman and David Stockton.

Warley signed with the Indiana Pacers’ G League affiliate, the Noblesville Boom, after agreeing to join the Eastern Conference franchise at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas, where he impressed coaches and front office personnel with his defensive play and versatility.

Grant-Foster didn’t stick with the San Antonio Spurs after a Summer League assignment, but managed to sign on with the Miami Heat’s G League squad, the Sioux Falls Skyforce, after being selected No. 15 overall during Saturday’s G League draft.

Entering his third professional season since leaving GU, Watson, a Gonzaga Prep product, is returning to the Los Angeles’ Lakers G League affiliate but will be playing home games in a different arena after the team switched from South Bay, playing in El Segundo, to Coachella Valley in Palm Desert.

Watson was one of South Bay’s top performers last year, averaging 11.3 points, 5.0 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.3 steals over 36 games and 24 starts.

Hickman is returning to the Capital City Go-Go (Washington Wizards) for the second season since going undrafted in 2025. The former Gonzaga guard was a part-time starter for Capital City last season, starting in 17 of 33 games, and averaged 10.8 ppg and 3.6 apg while shooting 43% from the field and 39.5% from the 3-point line.

Stockton, who recently agreed to a deal with the Valley Suns (Phoenix Suns), is back for his sixth stint in the G League after spending a year with Piratas de Quebradillas of the Baloncesto Superior Nacional in Puerto Rico. The former GU point guard and son of Gonzaga legend John Stockton played for the Valley Suns in 2024-25 and could share the court this season with Drew Timme, who’s on a two-way deal with Phoenix.

Timme is one of four ex-Zags who could split their time between the NBA and G League this season. Graham Ike (Golden State Warriors), Ryan Nembhard (Denver Nuggets) and Malachi Smith (Toronto Raptors) also entered the 2026-27 campaign on two-way contracts.

Guard Hunter Sallis, who played two seasons at Gonzaga before transferring to Wake Forest returns to the G League San Diego Clippers (Los Angeles Clippers), while wing Michael Ajayi, who spent a season in Spokane between stops at Pepperdine and Butler, is on a two-way deal with the Charlotte Hornets after going undrafted in June.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women see plenty of bright spots in exhibition rout of Westmont
Gonzaga.summary:
As exhibitions go, it was true to form.

Dig deeper and it’s clear to see why there’s excitement about two teams that play in McCarthey Athletic Center.

Nearly a month to the day of its first preseason practice, the Gonzaga women’s basketball team showed it was ready to play Tuesday, cruising past the NCAA Division II Westmont College Warriors 84-43 before 4,490.

All 12 available Gonzaga players saw time in the first half, and a freshman made an emphatic debut.

Abby Lusk, the Zags’ lone freshman from Pocatello, Idaho, made the first two shots of her career, both 3-pointers, and had 10 points on 4 of 4 shooting in five minutes.

Impressive considering she had been out a week after spraining an ankle. Coach Lisa Fortier said Lusk was a game-time decision.

“It’s the little things that, like, Little Me dreamed about,” Lusk said of her debut. “Getting your first college baskets. It’s just a surreal moment. Being able to make two (back-to-back 3-pointers) is kind of fun too. Seeing the love and support from the bench and the girls on the court … it was everything I envisioned it being.”

Lusk finished with 12 points and four rebounds in 11 minutes.

“We wanted to get her under the lights and see how she did,” Fortier said. “And she did very well. … I think her parents would have come up if they would have known she was going to play. But we had no idea.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who was the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season, scored Gonzaga’s first basket. Whittaker ate up the smaller Warriors inside in the opening 20 minutes with 16 points on 6-of-8 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. She finished with a game-high 24 points, six rebounds and three assists in 21 minutes.

Four of five starters from a year ago started Tuesday and Mead High graduate and junior guard Teryn Gardner stepped into the lineup, replacing fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt.

The lone Zag not to play was sophomore forward Jaiden Haile, who was the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year last season. She was wearing a boot from an overuse injury. She started shooting in light practice last week.

Every Gonzaga player logged at least 10 minutes.

Another bright spot was the play of senior guard Zeryhia Aokuso. She scored from all areas, finishing with 14 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga asserted authority early in the third quarter, using a 7-0 spurt to set the tone. It was the most pleasing stretch for Fortier.

“The thing I liked the most was how we came out in the third,” Fortier said. “Hopefully our team is going to be a team that gets leads and then play from the front versus always coming from behind. We talked at halftime about what our energy was going to look like in the third. I thought it was really good energy, probably our best quarter.”

It was the second game in two days for Westmont, from Santa Barbara, California. The Warriors fell 71-46 at Washington State on Sunday.

Gonzaga opens the season with three straight home games, beginning Monday when North Dakota State visits. The Bison are picked to win the Summit League championship.

NDSU is similar to Gonzaga. The Bison return four of five starters including a Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year.

Gonzaga opened the season at NDSU last year, winning 81-66.

“North Dakota State is really good,” Fortier said. “So it’s a tough opener. Hopefully we’ll get the best work we can in the next few days.”
